name: Horseradish root (in a fixed combination with nasturtium herb, by mouth)
short: Rats (not people): horseradish extract caused bladder-lining overgrowth and promoted bladder cancer; nasturtium harmed fetuses. With nasturtium in people: no significant difference from placebo.
text: All the human data are for a fixed combination of horseradish root and nasturtium herb taken by mouth, so no event can be credited to horseradish alone. In a phase III placebo-controlled trial in 217 women with recurrent cystitis taking the combination or placebo for 6 months, there were no significant differences between groups for any reported adverse effect. In a 90-day placebo-controlled trial in adults with chronically recurrent urinary tract infections (174 enrolled, of whom 45 were screening failures), 36 people on the combination and 37 on placebo reported adverse events; two serious adverse events occurred with placebo and one with the combination, which was not associated with the study medication. In a 351-adult placebo-controlled trial for preventing respiratory infections and a 96-patient trial against the antibiotic co-trimoxazole for acute cystitis, the combination was described as well tolerated; neither abstract gives event counts. In observational studies comparing it with antibiotics chosen by doctors, adverse events were recorded in 1.5% of 1,223 people of 4 years and over given the combination and 6.8% of 426 given antibiotics, and in 0.6% of 523 children and adolescents aged 4 to 18 given it and 3.9% of 335 given antibiotics; in 96 inpatients with catheter-associated urinary tract infections, adverse events and drug reactions occurred in 23.8% given it alone, 44.8% given it with antibiotics and 34.5% given antibiotics alone. These were not randomised comparisons. The trial abstracts do not say what the reported adverse events were. Irritation: a rat study describes horseradish extract as consisting mainly of allyl isothiocyanate (mustard oil) and other isothiocyanates. In experimental studies in people, mustard oil applied to the tongue caused oral irritation, and in an experiment in 60 healthy people, repeated nasal stimuli with it produced irritation; of 259 patients tested for suspected contact dermatitis from vegetables and food, 2 had a positive reaction to allyl isothiocyanate and 43 a doubtful one, and the authors say allergic contact dermatitis from it occurs in only a limited number of cases despite frequent exposure. These studies used mustard oil (allyl isothiocyanate), not horseradish root or the combination product. A 1988 letter, indexed as a case report and available as a title only, is titled 'Horseradish horrors: sushi syncope' (syncope means fainting); its title gives no further detail. Animal data (not people): in rats given a horseradish extract in drinking water for 13 weeks, overgrowth (hyperplasia) of the bladder lining was found in all treated groups; over 104 weeks it did not increase tumours apart from simple bladder-lining hyperplasia, but after a chemical that starts bladder cancer it increased bladder papillomas and carcinomas. In pregnant rats, high doses of a nasturtium extract were followed by fetal growth retardation and kidney damage. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
